full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and Opposite Party No.1 to show cause, why the judgment and order dated 28-3-95 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Dhaka in Criminal Appeal No. 150 of 1992 upholding the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 14-5-92 passed by the Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka in Petition Case No.18(A) of 92 corresponding to Case No. 456(A) of 91 convicting the petitioners under section 42 of the Forest (Amendment) Act, 1990 sentencing them thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 6 months and to pay a fine of Taka 3000 each in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one month, should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Short facts necessary for the purpose of this Rule, is that a petition of complaint was lodged on 28-4-91 by opposite party No.1 Syed Mortuza Ali, a forest Ranger, as complainant stating, inter alia, that on 28-2-91 at about 11-00 am he along with other witnesses having gone to Tejgaon Railway Station conducted a search in the Railway Wagon No. 54857 whereupon they found some 47 pieces of timber, Segun in kind, belonging to the accused persons, namely the petitioners herein, the petitioners could not show any valid document for those timbers, as such those pieces of timber were seized in presence of the accused persons, consequent whereupon the petition of complaint was lodged for contravention of Rules under section 41 of Forest Act, 1927 as amended in 1990; the seized pieces of timber, according to the complainant, measured 60 cubic feet worth about Taka 30,000. The seized articles were taken in the custody of Forest Department. On the basis of the said complaint, petition case No. 456A (1) of 1991 was initiated before the Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka. 

 3. The defence case as it appears from the deposition of DWs as also from the trend of cross-examination is that, the accused persons produced valid papers including Railway Receipt containing particulars of Transit Passes bearing No. 17/0005505 dated 13-10-90 and No. 81/0005372 dated 25-10-90, containing description of the timber in the said railway receipt showing payment of Taka 5,992 in favour of the Railway Department, but the Forest Officials did not pay heed to those papers rather demanded illegal gratification, which when refused by the accused persons, they have been falsely implicated in the instant case as a coercive measure. 

 4. The case was eventually tried by the learned Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka where six witnesses were examined on behalf of the prosecution while the defence adduced two witnesses in support of their respective cases and upon conclusion of the trial the learned Magistrate convicted the accused petitioners under sections 41 and 42 of the Forest Act, 1927 as amended under Forest (Amendment) Act, 1990 sentencing each of them thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 6 months with fine of Taka 3000 in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 1 month more, by his judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 14-5-92 in petition Case No. 456A(1) of 1991. 

 7. Mr Syed Abu Kowser Dabirusan, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing with Mr Alamgir Kabir, learned Assistant Attorney-General, at the outset raised a preliminary objection in this case as to the jurisdiction of this Court in entertaining the instant Revisional Application. The learned Deputy Attorney-General referring to the proviso to Rule 7 of Chapter-II Part-I of the Rules of High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, submitted that the impugned judgment as passed by the trial Court being a judgment of conviction and sentence with forfeiture, a Single Judge of this Court cannot hear the Rule rather the matter should be heard and disposed of by a Division Bench. 

 8. This question as raised by the learned Deputy Attorney-General being a pertinent one touching the jurisdiction of this Court, should be disposed of first before proceeding with the case any further. 

 10. It may not be out of place to mention that some 47 pieces of timber were seized by the Forest officials in view of the breach of the rules framed under section 41 of the Forest Act, 1927 and those timbers were sold before the trial had commenced in the case and the learned Magistrate by his aforesaid order disposed of the said sale proceeds as indicated above and from the said order the learned Deputy Attorney-General pointed out that the aforesaid expression as made in the ordering portion by the Magistrate is tantamount to forfeiture. Therefore, according to the learned Deputy Attorney-General, this Court sitting singly cannot hear the matter arising out of such a case. 

 17. Mr Masudur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has also relied upon a case of The Chairman of Bankura Municipality, Bankura vs Lalji Raja and Sons reported in AIR 1953 SC 248, where a similar question arose before the Indian Supreme Court as to whether the order passed by the District Magistrate, Bankura under sections 431 and 432, Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 amounted to an order of 'forfeiture' of property within the meaning of the proviso as available under the High Court Rules similar to those of our proviso available under Rule 7 Part-I Chapter-II of the Rules of the High Court Division, relevant portion of which may be quoted as under: 

 19. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also referred to the provision of section 42 of the Forest Act, 1927 as amended under the Forest (Amendment) Act, 1990 which contains penalty for breach of Rules made under section 41 which contains only imprisonment and fine and not forfeiture and, in view of the provisions of law as pointed out above, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the expression contained in the judgment of the trial Court in the instant case cannot under any stretch of imagination be termed as 'forfeiture' within the meaning of the proviso to the aforesaid Rules of the High Court Division. 

 22. Turning to the merit of the case, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits at the outset that the occurrence according to the prosecution, took place on 28-2-92 while the petition of complaint was lodged on 28-4-92 with a delay of about 2 months without disclosing any plausible explanation for the same and under such circumstances the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the delay in the instant case raises a serious doubt about the prosecution case rather it lends support to the defence version to the effect that the forest officials had waited for all this time to extract illegal gratification from the petitioners and having failed to obtain the same, lodged the instant case as a coercive measure and, in substantiating such submission, the learned Advocate for the petitioners placed reliance in the case of Md Siddiqur Rahman and others vs State reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 93, wherein it has been held by their Lordships that inordinate delay in filing the case raises doubt as to the manner, time and place of occurrence. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits further that non-production of the seized timber before the Court casts serious doubt as to the prosecution case, particularly on the point of alleged absence of hammer mark in the seized timber and that the disposal of those timbers without any specific order from the Court also raises a serious doubt as to the case of the prosecution and, in substantiating his submission, the learned Advocate for the petitioner placed reliance in the case of Bangladesh vs Paran Chandra Baroi reported in 1986 BCR (AD) 225, wherein it has been held by their Lordships in the Appellate Division to the effect that non-production of vital alamats raises a reasonable suspicion as to the credibility of witnesses. 

 23. The learned Advocate for the petitioners submits further that in the instant case the prosecution came up with two different versions—one at the initial stage and the other at the time of trial namely, the complainant initially lodged the complaint with the allegation that the accused persons could not produce any valid paper in support of the seized timbers and at a subsequent stage, at the time of trial, the prosecution raised the allegation to the effect that the seized timber did not contain any hammer mark. Under such circumstances, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that in a situation like this there are two different versions of the case—one in the evidence and other in the petition of complaint. In such circumstances no reliance should be placed on the evidence led by the complainant and in substantiating his submission the learned Advocate for the petitioner placed reliance in the case of Shajahan Biswas and others vs State reported in 40 DLR (AD) 291, wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division have held that the informant who gave direct evidence of the incident but the story given by him in Court is a complete departure from the one he had narrated in his ejhar so it is really difficult to place any reliance upon his evidence. 

 24. Lastly, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that in the instant case both the Courts below did not at all consider the defence version of the case. Rather it is incumbent upon the trial Court to consider the prosecution case vis-a-vis the defence case thereby acted illegally in passing the impugned judgments, substantiating his submission before the Court, the learned Advocate for the petitioners placed reliance in the case of Muslimuddin and others vs State reported in 38 DLR (AD) 311 wherein by a majority decision, their Lordships have held that the Court is obliged to carefully examine the prosecution case as well as the defence version and if it is found that the defence put forward on behalf of the accused has a reasonable possibility of being true the accused is entitled to a verdict of benefit of doubt. 

 25. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also submitted that in this case both the Courts below did not make any attempt to put the evidence in chief made by the witnesses with those of their cross-examination in juxtaposition with a view to seeing whether the witnesses stood the test of cross-examination whereby the Courts below misdirected themselves in coming to a correct decision in the case and, in substantiating his submission, the learned Advocate, for the petitioner placed reliance in the case of Wajear Rahman Moral vs State reported in 43 DLR (AD) 25, wherein their Lordships in the Appellate Division have held that the statements elicited from a witness in cross-examination, the most effective of all means ever invented for the discovery of truth and exposing falsehood, are a part, a very important part, of evidence before Court. Before drawing any inference from the testimony of a witness the Court, particularly the trial Court, must consider the statements made in chief and those made in cross by putting them in juxtaposition and see whether that witness has stood the test or supplied his own refutation. 

 26. Mr Syed Abu Kowser Dabirusan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing with Mr Md Alamgir Kabir, learned Assistant Attorney-General, submits that in the instant case when the forest officials challenged the petitioners at the railway station, they failed to produce the transit pass with respect to the seized timber which were being carried from Chittagong to Dhaka through railway wagon and conspicuous absence of any transit pass with the accused petitioners at the relevant time disclosed clear violation of rules framed under section 41 of the Forest Act, 1927 as amended under the Forest (Amendment) Act, 1990. Therefore, in view of gross violation of the rules the accused person has rightly been convicted by the trial Court and it was upheld by the Appellate Court. 

 29. It is also evident from the deposition of DW 1 to the effect that the railway receipt was duly produced before the forest officials when asked for and that the seized pieces of timber contained hammer marks. It is also on record that the prosecution admits that the railway receipt was duly produced before them. It appears from the Annexure-C the railway receipt where there is a clear reference to Transit pass No.17/0005505 dated 13-10-90 and Transit' Pass No. 81/ 0005372 dated 25-10-90 and that the said railway receipt contains description of 321 pieces of timber of different sizes and shapes. The prosecution has, however, alleged that the said railway receipt is not in connection with the seized timber, but there is no further details disclosed by the prosecution in the case as to how this railway receipt cannot be connected with the seized timbers. 

 30. The entire case, as made out by the prosecution, hinges on the point that the accused persons could not show valid papers in support of their possession of the seized timbers and that the timbers seized did not contain the hammer marks as required under section 41 of the Forest (Amendment) Act, 1927. From a close scrutiny of the materials on record it appears that the valid papers in support of their possession of the seized timber were duly produced before the forest officials but those were not heeded to, for reasons best known to them. It also appears that there is nothing on record, particularly in the order-sheet of the Magistrate, to dispose of the seized timber, during pendency of the trial. Despite such a position it appears further that the seized timbers were sold before the trial had commenced in the case. Therefore, none of the seized materials could be produced before the trial Court for arriving at a correct finding as to whether those contained hammer marks or not. It is also on record that in cross-examination DW 1 Borhanuddin disclosed to the effect: 

 31. It appears further that the Courts below did not apply their judicial mind to the cross-examination portion of the deposition of the witnesses as also the defence version of the case. Therefore, misdirected themselves in arriving at a correct conclusion in the instant case. It may be mentioned further that the appellate Court as a last Court of fact has also failed to consider, assess and evaluate the evidence on record as was desired of him. Consequently, upheld the erroneous decision of the trial Court. 

 32. Under the facts and circumstances stated above, it appears that the learned Advocate for the petitioners has rightly pointed out that in the instant case the Courts below have occasioned miscarriage of justice by ignoring the defence case as well as the cross-examination portion of the prosecution witnesses which, if considered carefully, would have indicated that the defence version of the case had been made probable and the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. 33. In the facts and circumstances of the case, it appears to me that the prosecution rather miserably failed to prove their case beyond reasonable doubt and, in that view of the matter, it is not the question of benefit of doubt under which the petitioners should be acquitted rather they should be acquitted honourably in view of the absence of reliable evidence on record for the prosecution.
